semantics.note: 'I can't imagine ... are really going to' is a firm statement of disbelief, not a probability hedge. The 'perhaps' only qualifies the narrow-use exception. The proposition keeps the scope and the exception. The 'let alone' clause about debugging is left out, but it only adds force and is not a separate core claim.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'prime time' as sustained real use with ordinary reliability and maintenance is fair and ordinary. Requiring documented builder background and outside help fits the noncoder scope. The contract correctly notes there is no deadline.

evidence.note: Lovable's own case study (Sep 2025) of a noncoder's app with 10k+ users and external integrations. It is a vendor disclosure. It does not check reliability, maintenance or engineering help, so under the contract it cannot settle the claim early.

Engineering firm's account (Mar 2026) of a noncoder-built app that became unstable and needed professional migration. It illustrates Marcus's concern, but a single case cannot settle a general forecast with no deadline.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm negative forecast with no deadline. Plinq (e1) is the closest counterexample, but it is a vendor account with no independent check of reliability, maintenance, or outside engineering help, so the early-resolution rule is not met. e2 points the other way but is a single case. Nothing in the packet settles the outcome.

attribution.note: Marcus asserts this in his own words. He then cites an embedded post as illustration, but the claim itself is his.

semantics.note: The proposition correctly isolates the factual assertion about coder frustration and Cursor's use of Claude. The rhetorical point about what the podcast omitted is excluded, which is appropriate.

contract.note: The readings of 'significant number' (substantial, not a majority) and 'deeply frustrated' (strong dissatisfaction) are fair plain readings. The Jan 1–Mar 2, 2025 window is the evaluator's choice but reasonable for a present-tense claim.

evidence.note: Cursor staff announcement (Feb 24, 2025) confirms that Claude powered Cursor, which supports only the parenthetical. The thread's few complaints sit alongside praise and say nothing about how widespread frustration was among working coders.

reviews.rationale: The Claude-integration point is supported by Cursor's own announcement. The core claim, that a significant number of working coders were deeply frustrated, has no survey or substantial body of firsthand reports in the packet from the target period. A handful of forum complaints cannot establish prevalence, so the main assertion is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. Hinton is quoted only as background; the replacement and shortage claims are Marcus's.

semantics.note: 'My understanding is' signals how confident he is in a factual report. It is not a probability hedge, so the claim is still a scored observation. The hedge and both parts (zero replacements, widespread shortages) are kept.

contract.note: Reading 'replaced' as job displacement rather than task substitution fits the context about training radiologists and is fair. Reading 'many parts of the world' as multiple countries or regions is ordinary.

evidence.note: Royal College of Radiologists census published June 2024: a 30% UK shortfall in radiology consultants. Supports the shortage part only.
RSNA report from Dec 2024 citing named US leaders who describe shortages at most academic institutions. Supports the shortage part in a second country. It is not a census.

Danish regional authority (Apr 2024): AI partly replaced one of two readers in breast screening, and the doctor moved to other duties. That is task substitution, not job loss, under the contract. It also notes a radiologist shortage.

reviews.rationale: Shortages in several countries (UK, US, Denmark) are well supported. The universal claim that not one radiologist was replaced has no positive evidence either way. e3 shows task substitution, not displacement, and finding no case of displacement does not prove there were none. Because the main zero-replacement part cannot be settled, the claim as a whole is unresolved; only the shortage part holds.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Are increasingly going to' is unhedged, so this is a scored forecast. Rendering 'naive enthusiasm from people like Roose' as AI coding hype is faithful. The US-children scope is kept, and no deadline was stated.

contract.note: Requiring measures over time of actual discouragement, plus evidence that AI enthusiasm caused it, is a fair plain reading. The contract correctly notes there is no endpoint.

evidence.note: HostingAdvice survey of 1,061 US adults, fielded Feb 2025: 88% would encourage others to learn to code. It is a single baseline taken before the post. It does not measure advice to children or any later trend.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm trend forecast with no deadline. The packet has only one survey from before the post and no repeated measurements of discouragement aimed at American children, nor any evidence on its cause. No conclusive event meets the early-resolution rule, so the outcome is unresolved.
